patient.name: Priya Ramanathan
patient.complaint: Painful, swollen left calf for 2 days
background: Flew home from Sydney 6 days ago (22-hour journey)
Takes the combined oral contraceptive pill
Accountant in Croydon; no previous clots

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a unilateral swollen calf after a flight, surgery or the pill, set against cellulitis and claudication; or 'Which risk factor most likely caused it?'.

points: Priya, 36, flew home from **Sydney** six days ago.
Two days of an aching, **tight left calf**.
Left leg swollen to the knee; worse on walking.
No breathlessness, chest pain or haemoptysis.

steps.lead: Priya's tight, swollen calf is most likely a **clot in a deep leg vein**; the danger is that it breaks off and travels to her lungs.
Priya has several **provoking** factors: a 22-hour flight, the **COCP** and obesity.

points: Left calf **4 cm** bigger than the right.
Pitting oedema to the knee; warm and mildly red.
Tender along the deep veins of the calf.
Dilated superficial veins over the shin.

steps.lead: Priya's warm, tender, swollen calf with **pitting oedema** and dilated superficial veins is the textbook picture.

steps.title: DVT vs its look-alikes
head: Feature
DVT
Cellulitis
Ruptured Baker's cyst
rows: Whole calf or leg, pitting, one side
Sudden calf pain after knee swelling

steps.q: Which feature most favours DVT over cellulitis in Priya?
o: Recent long-haul flight with pitting oedema
steps.r: Tenderness, warmth and redness occur in both. A **provoking risk factor** plus unilateral pitting oedema without fever points to DVT.

steps.lead: Priya has no breathlessness or chest pain now, but she must return at once if she develops them: that would be **PE**.

steps.text: A DVT patient who becomes **breathless, tachycardic or hypoxic** has a PE until proven otherwise. Do not call it anxiety.

steps.lead: If Priya had an **atrial septal defect**, a leg clot could cross to the left heart and cause a stroke: **paradoxical embolism**.
Priya's DVT is **provoked**. Had it come from nowhere, especially with weight loss, you would look for **cancer** or **thrombophilia**.

steps.text: Exam rule: **unilateral swollen calf + flight, surgery or the pill = DVT**. Fever with demarcated redness = cellulitis. Pain on walking relieved by rest = claudication.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?': the 2-level Wells score decides between D-dimer (score 1 or less) and proximal leg vein ultrasound (score 2 or more).

steps.title: 2-level Wells pathway for DVT
nodes: Suspected DVT: calculate the 2-level Wells score
Score ≥2 (likely) → proximal leg vein ultrasound within 4 h
No scan within 4 h → D-dimer plus interim DOAC
Negative D-dimer in low risk → DVT excluded
steps.caption: The score decides the first test, not the D-dimer.

steps.q: Priya has calf swelling ≥3 cm, pitting oedema in that leg and deep vein tenderness. What is her Wells score?
steps.r: One point each for **calf swelling ≥3 cm**, **pitting oedema** and **deep vein tenderness** = 3. A score of 2 or more means DVT likely.

visual.title: 2-level Wells score for DVT
visual.label: Priya 3
visual.caption: Priya is in the 'likely' band, so imaging comes first.

steps.lead: Priya scores **3: DVT likely**. She needs a proximal leg vein ultrasound within 4 hours, not a D-dimer as the decider.

points: It is 9 pm; ultrasound is not available until morning.
D-dimer sent; first dose of **apixaban** given.

steps.title: Bloods before anticoagulation
steps.text: Baseline FBC, renal function and clotting are checked before anticoagulation. The D-dimer is raised but cannot confirm a clot.

steps.lead: Next morning, **compression ultrasound** shows a non-compressible left popliteal vein: Priya's DVT is confirmed.
Had Priya's scan been normal with a positive D-dimer, you would **stop apixaban** and **rescan in 1 week**.
If Priya were pregnant, the test would still be ultrasound (**compression duplex**), with no radiation.

steps.text: A **negative D-dimer only excludes DVT in a low-probability patient**. D-dimer is also raised after surgery, in pregnancy, infection and cancer.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?': a DOAC first-line, LMWH in pregnancy or special cases, and the duration (3 months provoked, 6 months unprovoked or cancer).

steps.q: Priya's DVT is confirmed. She is well with normal renal function. What is first-line treatment?
steps.r: A **DOAC** (apixaban or rivaroxaban). Aspirin and stockings do not treat a DVT; warfarin always needs LMWH cover at the start.

steps.lead: Priya continues **apixaban**, a DOAC that blocks factor Xa. No bridging and no INR checks.
Priya is none of the special cases. In pregnancy, severe renal failure or cancer, **LMWH** or warfarin with LMWH cover would be chosen instead.

steps.title: Anticoagulants for DVT
head: DOAC
LMWH
Warfarin
rows: DOAC unsuitable; needs LMWH ≥5 days first

steps.lead: Priya's DVT was **provoked** by a flight (a transient non-surgical factor), so she has **3 months** of apixaban.

steps.title: How long to anticoagulate
nodes: Provoked by a transient non-surgical factor → 3 months

points: Advised to **stop the COCP**; switch to non-oestrogen contraception.
Given written advice on PE symptoms.
Review at 3 months to stop apixaban.

steps.lead: Priya is told to call 999 for sudden breathlessness or chest pain. Surgical patients get **pneumatic compression** at once and **LMWH 12 hours post-op**.

visual.title: Priya's calf on apixaban
visual.caption: Swelling settles over weeks. Anticoagulation stops new clot forming; the body's own fibrinolysis clears the old clot.

steps.lead: Priya's pathway (Wells, a 4-hour scan, interim DOAC, then 3 months of apixaban) follows **NICE NG158**.

steps.text: Do not treat a DVT with **aspirin** or stockings. Treatment is anticoagulation; aspirin is an antiplatelet for arterial disease.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: which part of Virchow's triad a vignette shows, how DOACs work, and why a DVT leads to PE or post-thrombotic syndrome.

steps.title: Virchow's triad in Priya
nodes: Endothelial injury: surgery or trauma (none for Priya)
Slow flow in calf valve pockets

steps.lead: Priya ticks two corners of **Virchow's triad**: stasis from the flight and hypercoagulability from oestrogen.
Priya's red, warm, swollen calf is **inflammation** plus blocked venous outflow from the popliteal clot.
A popliteal clot is **proximal**, the kind most likely to propagate and **embolise** to Priya's lungs.

steps.text: **Proximal** DVTs (popliteal vein and above) carry the highest embolic risk, which is why the scan targets the proximal veins.

steps.title: Where apixaban acts
nodes: Apixaban and rivaroxaban block factor Xa

steps.q: How does apixaban stop Priya's clot growing?
steps.r: Apixaban **directly inhibits factor Xa**. Heparins work via antithrombin, warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling, aspirin blocks COX-1.

steps.lead: Blocking **factor Xa** means less thrombin is made, so Priya's clot stops extending.
If Priya's vein valves are left leaky, high venous pressure causes **post-thrombotic syndrome**: aching, swelling, pigmentation and ulcers.

mcq.q: Which new symptom in a DVT patient suggests pulmonary embolism?
mcq.r: Sudden breathlessness, **pleuritic chest pain**, collapse or tachycardia mean PE: emergency assessment.

mcq.q: Which cardiac defect lets a leg DVT cause a stroke?
mcq.r: An **ASD** lets venous clot cross right to left: **paradoxical embolism**.

mcq.q: An unprovoked DVT in a 65 year old should prompt assessment for which condition?
mcq.r: Unprovoked or recurrent DVT should prompt a search for **malignancy** or **thrombophilia**.
**≥2 = likely**: proximal leg vein ultrasound within 4 hours. ≤1 = unlikely: D-dimer.

mcq.q: Which is the best initial test when the Wells score is 1 or less?
mcq.r: **D-dimer**: a negative result in a low-risk patient rules out DVT.

mcq.q: Ultrasound is negative but the D-dimer is positive. What next?
o: Stop anticoagulation and rescan in 1 week
mcq.r: **Stop anticoagulation and repeat the scan in 1 week** to catch a propagating calf clot.

mcq.q: Which is first-line treatment for a confirmed DVT?
mcq.r: A **DOAC** (apixaban or rivaroxaban), which inhibits factor Xa.

mcq.q: How long is anticoagulation for a DVT provoked by long-haul travel?
mcq.r: Provoked by a transient non-surgical factor: **3 months**. Unprovoked: 6 months.

mcq.q: When is prophylactic-dose LMWH started after surgery?
mcq.r: **12 hours post-op**, with an intermittent pneumatic compression device straight away.

mcq.q: Which long-term complication of DVT comes from venous valve incompetence?
mcq.r: **Post-thrombotic syndrome**: persistent venous hypertension and leaky valves.

prompts.q: What is a DVT and why does it matter?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the clot, the place and the danger.

points.p: A blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the leg
points.why: Proximal (popliteal and above) clots matter most.
This explains the swelling, warmth and redness.

points.p: Can embolise to the lungs as a pulmonary embolism
points.why: PE is the major life-threatening complication.

prompts.q: List the risk factors for DVT.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem usually hides one strong risk factor among weak ones like smoking or alcohol.

points.why: Venous stasis from hours of sitting.
Even minor surgery in recent weeks counts in the exam.
Use compression duplex ultrasound to investigate.
Stop the COCP after a DVT.
Cancer is also a major risk factor.

prompts.q: What do you find on examining a leg with a DVT?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one leg, whole calf, pitting, no fever.

points.why: Calf ≥3 cm bigger than the other scores a Wells point.
Also seen in cellulitis, so look for fever and demarcation.
Pitting oedema of the symptomatic leg scores a Wells point.
Blood diverts around the blocked deep vein.

prompts.q: Which features tell you a DVT has become a PE?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: new chest symptoms in a leg patient mean emergency assessment.

points.why: The most common PE symptom.
Sharp pain worse on inspiration.
Sinus tachycardia is the commonest ECG finding in PE.
Collapse or hypotension suggests massive PE.

prompts.q: When should a DVT make you look for a hidden cause, and what cause?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: no trigger, weight loss or a young patient with recurrence.

points.why: Unprovoked DVT also changes the duration to 6 months.

points.p: Recurrent DVT or a young patient
points.why: Think thrombophilia.
Weight loss or anaemia in the stem points here.
Family history of clots is the clue.

prompts.q: How can a leg DVT cause a stroke?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: venous clot can only reach the brain through a right-to-left shunt.

points.why: A bubble-contrast echo shows the shunt.
Clot crosses from the right to the left heart, bypassing the lungs.

prompts.q: Walk through the 2-level Wells pathway for suspected DVT.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the score decides the first test.

points.why: The scan should happen within 4 hours.
The time window is a favourite exam detail.

points.p: If no scan within 4 h: interim DOAC plus D-dimer
points.why: Do not leave a likely DVT untreated overnight.
D-dimer is sensitive but not specific.

points.p: Negative D-dimer in low risk rules out DVT
points.why: A positive D-dimer then needs ultrasound.

prompts.q: What is the gold-standard test, and what if it is negative but the D-dimer is positive?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ultrasound confirms; a negative scan may need repeating.

points.p: Compression (proximal leg vein) ultrasound is gold standard
points.why: A non-compressible vein means clot.
No confirmed clot, so no ongoing anticoagulation.
Catches a calf clot that propagates proximally.
No radiation needed.

prompts.q: What is first-line treatment for DVT, the alternatives, and how long for?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: drug first, then the provoked/unprovoked/cancer duration.

points.why: No INR monitoring needed.

points.p: If DOAC unsuitable: LMWH or warfarin pathway (pregnancy, severe renal impairment, cancer)
points.why: LMWH is the choice in pregnancy.

points.p: Warfarin needs LMWH for at least 5 days until INR 2–3
points.why: Warfarin is briefly prothrombotic at the start.
Long-haul travel or minor trauma.

points.p: Unprovoked: 6 months; active cancer: DOAC 6 months
points.why: Longer if recurrent or ongoing risk.

prompts.q: How is VTE prevented in surgical patients?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: mechanical straight away, drug 12 hours later.

points.why: Mechanical prophylaxis has no bleeding risk.
Waiting 12 hours limits surgical bleeding.

prompts.q: Explain Virchow's triad and why clots form in the calf.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: map each stem risk factor to one corner of the triad.

points.why: A long flight is pure stasis.
Surgery is the classic example.
The COCP is the classic exam example.

points.p: Slow flow in valve pockets of calf veins activates the cascade
points.why: That is why the calf is the commonest site.

prompts.q: How do DOACs work, and what long-term problem can follow a DVT?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the factor, then the valve damage.

points.why: Dabigatran is the exception: a direct thrombin inhibitor.

points.p: Less thrombin generated, so the clot stops propagating
points.why: They do not dissolve the clot; fibrinolysis does.
Aching, swelling, pigmentation and venous ulcers.

points.p: From venous hypertension and valve incompetence
points.why: The clot scars the valves it formed on.

glossary.DVT: Deep vein thrombosis: a blood clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg.
glossary.PE: Pulmonary embolism: a clot blocking a pulmonary artery, usually travelled from a leg DVT.
glossary.VTE: Venous thromboembolism: the umbrella term for DVT and PE.
glossary.Virchow's triad: The three causes of thrombosis: venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability.
glossary.Wells score: A clinical score of DVT probability; 2 or more means DVT likely.
glossary.D-dimer: A breakdown product of fibrin; sensitive for clot but raised in many other conditions.
glossary.compression ultrasound: Ultrasound where the probe presses on the vein; a vein that will not compress contains clot.
glossary.duplex ultrasound: Ultrasound combining an image of the vein with Doppler flow measurement.
glossary.proximal leg vein ultrasound: Ultrasound of the popliteal and femoral veins, where dangerous clots sit.
glossary.FEU: Fibrinogen-equivalent units, a unit used to report D-dimer.
glossary.DOAC: Direct oral anticoagulant, such as apixaban or rivaroxaban; no INR monitoring needed.
glossary.apixaban: A DOAC that directly inhibits factor Xa; first-line for DVT.
glossary.rivaroxaban: A DOAC that directly inhibits factor Xa; first-line for DVT.
glossary.LMWH: Low molecular weight heparin, a subcutaneous anticoagulant such as enoxaparin; used in pregnancy.
glossary.warfarin: An oral vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant monitored by the INR.
glossary.INR: International normalised ratio: a measure of warfarin effect; target 2 to 3 for DVT.
glossary.factor Xa: Activated factor X, the clotting factor that converts prothrombin to thrombin.
glossary.thrombin: The enzyme that turns fibrinogen into fibrin to form a clot.
glossary.antithrombin: A natural anticoagulant protein that heparins enhance.
glossary.COCP: Combined oral contraceptive pill; its oestrogen raises clotting risk.
glossary.HRT: Hormone replacement therapy; oestrogen-containing HRT raises clotting risk.
glossary.thrombophilia: An inherited or acquired tendency to form clots, such as factor V Leiden.
glossary.provoked DVT: A DVT with a clear trigger such as surgery, travel or immobility.
glossary.unprovoked DVT: A DVT with no clear trigger; prompts a look for cancer or thrombophilia.
glossary.paradoxical embolism: A venous clot crossing a heart defect to the arterial side, causing a stroke.
glossary.atrial septal defect: A hole between the two atria that can allow right-to-left passage of clot.
glossary.post-thrombotic syndrome: Chronic leg aching, swelling, pigmentation and ulcers after DVT from damaged vein valves.
glossary.pitting oedema: Swelling that keeps a dent after you press it with a finger.
glossary.intermittent pneumatic compression: Inflatable leg sleeves that squeeze the calves to keep blood moving after surgery.
glossary.popliteal vein: The deep vein behind the knee; a clot here is a proximal DVT.
glossary.proximal DVT: A clot in the popliteal vein or above; the highest risk of PE.
glossary.cellulitis: Bacterial skin infection with fever and spreading, well-demarcated redness.
glossary.Baker's cyst: A fluid-filled swelling behind the knee; rupture mimics DVT.
glossary.thrombophlebitis: Inflammation and clot in a superficial vein, felt as a tender red cord.
glossary.pleuritic: Chest pain that is sharp and worse on breathing in.
glossary.embolise: When a clot breaks off and travels in the blood to block a vessel elsewhere.
glossary.antiphospholipid syndrome: An autoimmune thrombophilia causing venous and arterial clots and miscarriages.
glossary.claudication: Calf pain on walking relieved by rest, from arterial narrowing.

technique.stem: A 41 year old woman has a 3 day history of a painful, swollen right calf. She returned from a flight from Singapore 1 week ago and takes the combined oral contraceptive pill. Her temperature is 37.2°C. Her right calf is 3.5 cm larger than her left, with pitting oedema and tenderness along the deep veins. She is not breathless.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about a swollen leg: decide clot, infection or musculoskeletal.

clues: returned from a flight from Singapore 1 week ago
steps.x: Two **provoking factors** (flight, oestrogen), no fever, whole-calf pitting swelling and deep vein tenderness.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Unilateral swollen calf after a flight on the pill: **DVT**.

elim: Baker's cyst rupture is sudden calf pain after a knee swelling, often with ankle bruising.
Cellulitis needs fever and well-demarcated spreading erythema.
A strain follows exertion and gives localised muscle pain, not pitting oedema.
Thrombophlebitis is a tender red cord along a superficial vein.

steps.x: **C. Deep vein thrombosis.** Rule: one swollen calf + flight, surgery or pill = DVT.

technique.stem: A 63 year old man has a 2 day history of a swollen, aching left leg. His left ankle was in a plaster cast for 5 weeks until last week. His left calf is 4 cm larger than his right and tender along the deep veins. His pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. The ultrasound department can scan him within 2 hours.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: An investigation question for suspected DVT: work out the Wells score first.
Cast immobilisation 1, calf swelling ≥3 cm 1, deep vein tenderness 1: **Wells 3, DVT likely**. A scan is available inside 4 hours.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Wells ≥2 with a scan inside 4 hours: **proximal leg vein ultrasound**.

elim: CTPA is for suspected PE; he has no chest symptoms and normal saturations.
D-dimer is first only when Wells is 1 or less, or as an interim test if the scan is delayed.
MR venography is not a first-line test for leg DVT.
Troponin has no role in diagnosing DVT.

steps.x: **D. Proximal leg vein ultrasound.** Rule: Wells ≥2 = scan within 4 hours.

technique.stem: A 29 year old woman has a proximal deep vein thrombosis confirmed on ultrasound. It started 4 days after a 14-hour flight. She is otherwise well, not pregnant and has no history of cancer. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Management: choose the drug, then the duration.
A **provoked** DVT (transient non-surgical factor), no pregnancy, no cancer, normal renal function: a DOAC is suitable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **DOAC for 3 months**.

elim: 6 months is for unprovoked or cancer-associated DVT.
Aspirin is not a treatment for DVT.
Lifelong anticoagulation is for antiphospholipid syndrome or recurrent VTE, not one provoked clot.
LMWH is for pregnancy or when a DOAC is unsuitable, and 6 weeks is too short.

steps.x: **A. Apixaban for 3 months.** Rule: provoked = 3 months, unprovoked or cancer = 6 months.

technique.stem: A 47 year old man develops a swollen left calf 5 days after a 20-hour flight. A deep vein thrombosis is confirmed. He has no personal or family history of clots, has had no recent surgery or injury and takes no medication.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his thrombosis?
o: Platelet activation on a ruptured plaque

steps.x: A mechanism question: map the risk factor in the stem to Virchow's triad.

clues: no personal or family history of clots
steps.x: The only risk factor is prolonged sitting. No thrombophilia, no injury, no oestrogen.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Long-haul travel = **venous stasis**.

elim: An inherited thrombophilia is unlikely with no personal or family history.
Endothelial injury needs surgery or trauma; he has had neither.
Nothing in the stem suggests cancer.
Plaque rupture causes arterial thrombosis (MI, stroke), not DVT.

steps.x: **E. Venous stasis.** Rule: travel and immobility = stasis; surgery = injury; pill, pregnancy, cancer = hypercoagulability.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has a 4 day history of a swollen, aching right leg. He had a right total hip replacement 3 weeks ago. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 136/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. The whole right leg is swollen with pitting oedema to the thigh and dilated superficial veins. The skin is intact.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Recent hip surgery plus a whole swollen leg with pitting oedema and dilated superficial veins is a DVT. Cellulitis needs fever and spreading demarcated erythema.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a swollen leg after surgery.
Major orthopaedic surgery is a strong **provoking factor**; no fever; collateral superficial veins mean deep venous obstruction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Post-op unilateral leg swelling: **DVT**.

elim: No fever, no skin break and no demarcated erythema.
Lymphoedema is chronic, non-pitting and slowly progressive.
Joint infection gives a hot painful hip, fever and wound signs, not whole-leg oedema.
A ruptured Baker's cyst gives sudden calf pain, not thigh swelling after surgery.

steps.x: **B. Deep vein thrombosis.** Rule: surgery in the last few weeks + one swollen leg = DVT.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman has a deep vein thrombosis of the left leg confirmed on ultrasound. She has not travelled or had surgery. She started the combined oral contraceptive pill 2 months ago. She smokes 5 cigarettes a day and drinks 10 units of alcohol a week. Her BMI is 23 kg/m².
practice.q: Which is the most likely risk factor for her DVT?
practice.e: Oestrogen in the COCP causes hypercoagulability and is a recognised DVT risk factor. Light smoking, modest alcohol and a normal BMI are weak or no risk.

steps.x: Pick the strongest risk factor among several.

clues: started the combined oral contraceptive pill 2 months ago
steps.x: Recent **oestrogen** exposure; the usual provokers are absent; BMI is normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **COCP**: oestrogen-induced hypercoagulability.

elim: 10 units a week is not a DVT risk factor.
A BMI of 23 is normal; obesity would be the risk.
Female sex alone is not the risk; oestrogen is.
Smoking is a weak VTE risk compared with oestrogen.

steps.x: **C. COCP.** Rule: in a young woman, the pill is the risk factor the exam wants.

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman was diagnosed with a left popliteal deep vein thrombosis 2 days ago. She now has sudden breathlessness and sharp right-sided chest pain worse on inspiration. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A proximal DVT followed by sudden breathlessness, pleuritic pain, tachycardia and hypoxia is a PE, the major complication of DVT. Pneumothorax would not follow a DVT and pericarditis is eased by leaning forward.

steps.x: Diagnosis of acute chest symptoms in a patient with a known DVT.

clues: popliteal deep vein thrombosis 2 days ago
steps.x: Proximal DVT + sudden pleuritic pain + **tachycardia and hypoxia**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The clot has embolised: **pulmonary embolism**.

elim: ACS gives central crushing pain, not pleuritic pain after a DVT.
Musculoskeletal pain does not cause hypoxia or tachycardia.
Pericarditis is positional and eased by sitting forward.
A pneumothorax has no link to a leg clot and would need a trigger.

steps.x: **E. Pulmonary embolism.** Rule: DVT + new breathlessness = PE until proven otherwise.

practice.stem: A 24 year old man has sudden weakness of his right arm and face. He was diagnosed with a left calf deep vein thrombosis 3 days ago after a long coach journey. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and regular and BP 124/76 mmHg. A bubble-contrast echocardiogram shows right-to-left shunting across the interatrial septum.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his stroke?
practice.e: A venous clot crossing an atrial septal defect into the arterial circulation is a paradoxical embolism. His pulse is regular, so atrial fibrillation is unlikely.

steps.x: Cause of a stroke in a young man with a recent DVT.

clues: calf deep vein thrombosis 3 days ago
pulse rate is 76 bpm and regular
right-to-left shunting across the interatrial septum
steps.x: Young, a venous clot, and a **shunt** across the atrial septum.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: DVT clot crossing an ASD: **paradoxical embolism**.

elim: The pulse is regular.
Dissection follows neck trauma with neck pain or Horner's syndrome.
Small vessel disease affects older hypertensive patients.
Vasculitis has systemic features, none given.

steps.x: **C. Paradoxical embolism.** Rule: DVT + stroke + ASD = paradoxical embolism.

practice.stem: A 59 year old man had a left femoral deep vein thrombosis 2 years ago. He now has aching and heaviness in the left leg that is worse at the end of the day. There is swelling, brown pigmentation and eczema around the medial ankle. Foot pulses are easily palpable. The calf is not tender.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Chronic aching, swelling and pigmentation years after a DVT is post-thrombotic syndrome from venous hypertension and damaged valves. Palpable pulses exclude arterial disease.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a chronic leg problem after a DVT.

clues: worse at the end of the day
brown pigmentation and eczema around the medial ankle
steps.x: Chronic **venous hypertension** signs years after a DVT; arterial supply intact; no acute clot features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Damaged valves after a DVT: **post-thrombotic syndrome**.

elim: Pulses are palpable; arterial disease gives claudication and cold pale feet.
Cellulitis is acute with fever and spreading erythema.
Lymphoedema does not cause haemosiderin pigmentation and venous eczema.
A new DVT is acute with a tender swollen calf, not a 2-year story.

steps.x: **D. Post-thrombotic syndrome.** Rule: old DVT + venous skin changes = post-thrombotic syndrome.

practice.stem: A 67 year old man has a right calf deep vein thrombosis confirmed on ultrasound. He has not travelled, had surgery or been immobile. He has lost 6 kg over 3 months and has had looser stools for 2 months.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his DVT?
practice.e: An unprovoked DVT with weight loss, change in bowel habit and iron deficiency anaemia points to occult colorectal cancer. Polycythaemia vera would give a high, not low, haemoglobin.

steps.x: Cause of an unprovoked DVT.

clues: not travelled, had surgery or been immobile
steps.x: **Unprovoked** DVT + weight loss + bowel change + iron deficiency anaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Malignancy-related hypercoagulability: **colorectal cancer**.

elim: Antiphospholipid syndrome fits younger patients with miscarriages or arterial clots.
Factor V Leiden presents young with a family history, not weight loss.
Nephrotic syndrome needs oedema and proteinuria.
Polycythaemia vera raises the haemoglobin; his is low.

steps.x: **B. Colorectal carcinoma.** Rule: unprovoked DVT + red flags = look for cancer.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has a 1 day history of mild aching in her left calf. Her calves measure the same, there is no oedema and no visible veins, but she is tender along the deep veins. She has no cancer, recent surgery or immobilisation. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. Her 2-level Wells score is 1.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: With a Wells score of 1 or less (DVT unlikely), D-dimer comes first; a negative result rules out DVT. Ultrasound first is for a score of 2 or more.

steps.x: First investigation for suspected DVT: use the Wells score given.
**Wells 1 = DVT unlikely.**

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Low probability: **D-dimer** first.

elim: CT venography is not a first-line leg DVT test.
MR venography is not first-line.
Ultrasound first is for Wells ≥2, or after a positive D-dimer.
Thrombophilia testing is not a diagnostic test for an acute clot.

steps.x: **B. D-dimer.** Rule: Wells ≤1 = D-dimer; negative = DVT excluded.

practice.stem: A 50 year old man with suspected left leg deep vein thrombosis had a 2-level Wells score of 2. Ultrasound was not available overnight, so he was given rivaroxaban. Today, a proximal leg vein ultrasound is normal. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Stop rivaroxaban and repeat ultrasound in 1 week
practice.e: A negative ultrasound with a positive D-dimer means stop anticoagulation and rescan in 1 week. Discharging him would miss a calf clot that propagates.

steps.x: Next step after a negative scan.

clues: proximal leg vein ultrasound is normal
steps.x: DVT likely, **scan negative**, **D-dimer positive**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Stop anticoagulation and rescan in 1 week.**

elim: There is no confirmed clot to treat.
He has no chest symptoms to suggest PE.
Positive D-dimer means a clot is not yet excluded.
Repeating the D-dimer adds nothing; it will still be raised.

steps.x: **E. Stop and rescan in 1 week.** Rule: scan negative + D-dimer positive = repeat scan at 1 week.

practice.stem: A 38 year old man has a proximal deep vein thrombosis confirmed on ultrasound after a 12-hour coach journey. He is otherwise well with no bleeding history. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: A DOAC such as apixaban is first-line for a stable DVT with normal renal and liver function. Warfarin alone is wrong because it needs LMWH cover for at least 5 days.

steps.x: First-line treatment of a confirmed DVT.
Confirmed clot, low bleeding risk, normal kidneys: a **DOAC** is suitable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Apixaban** (or rivaroxaban).

elim: Aspirin is an antiplatelet; it does not treat VTE.
Stockings do not treat a DVT.
UFH infusion is for severe renal failure or massive PE.
Warfarin must start with LMWH for at least 5 days until INR 2–3.

steps.x: **A. Apixaban.** Rule: DOAC first-line for DVT.

practice.stem: A 54 year old woman has a left femoral deep vein thrombosis with no identifiable trigger. History, examination and initial tests show no sign of cancer. She has started apixaban and asks how long she will need it.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate duration of anticoagulation?
practice.e: An unprovoked DVT is treated for 6 months, longer if recurrent or with ongoing risk. Three months is for a DVT provoked by a transient factor.

steps.x: Duration question: decide provoked, unprovoked or cancer.
**Unprovoked**, no cancer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Unprovoked DVT: **6 months**.

elim: 3 months is for a provoked DVT.
6 weeks is too short for any DVT.
Lifelong is for antiphospholipid syndrome or recurrent VTE.
Symptoms are not how duration is decided.

steps.x: **B. 6 months.** Rule: provoked 3, unprovoked 6, cancer 6.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man has just returned to the ward after an elective open right hemicolectomy. There were no bleeding problems in theatre. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 130/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate VTE prophylaxis?
practice.e: Surgical patients get an intermittent pneumatic compression device straight away, with prophylactic-dose LMWH from 12 hours post-op. Treatment-dose LMWH is for an established clot.

steps.x: Immediate DVT prevention after surgery.
Straight out of major abdominal surgery: **mechanical** first, drug at 12 hours.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Intermittent pneumatic compression** now; LMWH at 12 hours.

elim: A treatment DOAC is not post-op prophylaxis straight after surgery.
Aspirin is not the standard post-op prophylaxis here.
Waiting until mobile leaves him unprotected at peak risk.
Treatment-dose LMWH is for an established clot and risks bleeding.

steps.x: **C. IPC device.** Rule: mechanical now, prophylactic LMWH from 12 hours post-op.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman is started on rivaroxaban for a deep vein thrombosis after knee surgery. She asks how the tablet stops the clot getting bigger.
practice.q: Which is the mechanism of action of rivaroxaban?
o: Inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase
practice.e: Rivaroxaban and apixaban directly inhibit factor Xa, reducing thrombin generation and clot propagation. Dabigatran is the direct thrombin inhibitor.

steps.x: Drug mechanism for a DOAC.
The **-xaban** ending means anti-**Xa**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Direct factor Xa inhibition**.

elim: Heparins work by activating antithrombin.
Dabigatran is the direct thrombin inhibitor.
Clopidogrel blocks P2Y12; it is an antiplatelet.
That is warfarin.

steps.x: **B. Direct factor Xa inhibition.** Rule: -xaban = anti-Xa; -gatran = anti-thrombin.
